title: Stroke (Cerebrovascular Accident)
lead: Rebuilding movement after brain injury: assessment, recovery and task-specific training.

blocks.text: A stroke is a sudden loss of brain function caused by interrupted blood supply: **ischaemic** (a blocked artery, most strokes) or **haemorrhagic** (bleeding). Brain cells in the affected area die or stop working, causing weakness, sensory loss, speech, vision, swallowing and cognitive problems depending on the area. Recovery happens through neuroplasticity, the brain's ability to reorganise, which is strongly driven by intensive, repeated, meaningful practice [Ref – to verify].

rows: Opposite-side weakness and sensory loss, arm and face worse than leg; aphasia (left hemisphere) or neglect (right hemisphere)
Opposite leg weaker than arm; behavioural change
Vertigo, ataxia, visual field loss, double vision, swallowing problems
Pure motor or pure sensory stroke, no cortical signs

blocks.text: **Acute recognition (BE-FAST)**: **B**alance loss, **E**yes (vision loss), **F**ace drooping, **A**rm weakness, **S**peech difficulty, **T**ime to call emergency services.

items: Weakness (hemiparesis) and loss of selective movement.
Altered tone: low tone early, spasticity later in some patients.
Sensory and proprioceptive loss.
Balance and gait impairment, falls.
Shoulder pain and subluxation in the weak arm.
Neglect (ignoring one side of space), pusher behaviour (pushing toward the weak side).
Fatigue, low mood, cognitive and communication problems.

sections.title: C. Ask the right questions (patient, family, notes)

rows: Type of stroke, date, side, imaging, treatment (thrombolysis, thrombectomy)?
Blood pressure targets and medical restrictions?
Previous walking ability, home, stairs, carers?
Swallowing status (nil by mouth, modified diet)?
Aspiration risk during positioning and exercise
How to teach and give instructions

items: Vital signs (BP before and after activity).
Consciousness and cognition (follow commands, orientation).
Communication: comprehension and expression.
Tone: passive movement at slow and fast speeds; Modified Ashworth Scale.
Motor control and strength: selective movement, MRC grades, synergies.
Sensation: light touch, proprioception (joint position sense).
Neglect: line bisection, cancellation tasks, observation.
Shoulder: subluxation (finger-width gap below the acromion), pain, range.
Function: rolling, lying to sitting, sitting balance, sit-to-stand, standing, transfers, gait.
Standardised measures (Section E).

sections.title: E. Standardised measures (the "special tests" of neurology)

rows: Move the limb through range in about one second; grade 0, 1, 1+, 2, 3, 4
Motor recovery of arm and leg
Static and dynamic balance; 14 items, 0 to 56
Lower scores indicate higher falls risk [Ref – to verify cut-off]
Time the middle 6 m at comfortable speed

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: Gait speed is called the "sixth vital sign". It is simple, reliable and linked to community walking ability. Measure it at every reassessment.

sections.title: F. Differential diagnosis and related presentations

rows: New stroke or TIA during rehabilitation
Episodes of jerking or loss of awareness

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: New face, arm or speech change, sudden vision loss or imbalance
Call emergency team; note time of onset
BP above the medically agreed limit, severe headache
Coughing or wet voice during eating or drinking, fever
Hot, swollen painful hand and wrist

steps: **Medically stable?** (vital signs within orders, no deterioration in the last 24 hours) No: positioning, chest care, passive range. Yes: continue.
**Early mobilisation:** short, frequent out-of-bed sessions as the stroke team advises. Very intensive mobilisation within the first 24 hours is not recommended [Ref – to verify AVERT trial].
**Identify the main limitation** (sitting balance, transfers, walking, arm use).
**Set task-specific goals** and practise those tasks with high repetition.
**Reassess** weekly with gait speed, Berg, and arm measures.

sections.title: I. Hands-on techniques in stroke rehabilitation

rows: Facilitated movement (guiding the patient through a task)
Help the patient feel a correct movement
Early, when the patient cannot move alone
Reduce help as soon as possible; active practice is the aim
Weight-bearing through the weak arm in sitting
Sensory input, trunk and arm support
Never pull on the weak arm; support the arm at all times

blocks.text: **Core principles**: task-specific, repetitive, progressively challenging, meaningful to the patient, and in high dose.

rows: Reaching tasks in sitting outside the base of support
3 sets of 10 reaches in different directions
Repeated sit-to-stand from a raised seat, lowering seat height as able
Progressive resistance training (step-ups, leg press, bridging)
2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12, 2 to 3 times a week
Overground walking practice, treadmill with or without body-weight support, circuit class training
Arm with some wrist and finger movement
Constraint-induced movement therapy (restrain the strong arm, intensive use of the weak arm) [Ref – to verify criteria]
Hours of practice per day in structured programs
Mirror therapy, electrical stimulation, mental practice, bilateral tasks

blocks.label: COMMON STUDENT TRAP
body: Waiting for "normal" movement before allowing functional practice slows recovery. Allow the patient to practise real tasks, giving feedback on safety and quality.

rows: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) for foot drop or shoulder
Improves walking or reduces subluxation in some patients [Ref – to verify]
For foot drop and knee control
Avoid long-term slings that encourage stiffness
Combine with stretching and task practice

items: Acute (days): stability, positioning, swallowing awareness, early graded mobilisation, chest care, prevention of complications.
Subacute (weeks to months): intensive task-specific practice; most rapid recovery occurs in the first months [Ref – to verify].
Chronic (after about 6 months): continued gains possible with practice; fitness, community walking, secondary prevention (exercise, BP control).

blocks.text: Gait speed, 6MWT, Berg, Fugl-Meyer, Modified Ashworth, Barthel Index, goal attainment, falls diary.

blocks.label: CLINICAL CASE
body: A 64-year-old man is 10 days after a left middle cerebral artery ischaemic stroke. He has right arm weakness (some wrist extension), right leg weakness, expressive aphasia, and can sit unsupported but needs help of one to stand. BP stable within targets. Goal: walk to the bathroom.

blocks.text: > Plan: repeated sit-to-stand, standing balance tasks, assisted walking practice with a frame or therapist, right arm task practice (reaching, grasping cups), simple gestures and demonstrations to overcome aphasia.

items: **Why use demonstrations with this patient?** Expressive aphasia mainly affects speaking; comprehension may be better, but short instructions with demonstration are clearer.
**Which arm intervention could be considered later?** Constraint-induced movement therapy, because he has some active wrist extension.
**How do you protect his shoulder?** Support the arm, avoid pulling, position carefully, educate carers.
**Which measure do you take weekly for walking?** Gait speed (10-metre walk test).
**He suddenly develops slurred speech and facial droop in therapy. Action?** Emergency: possible new stroke; call the medical team and record the time.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Recognise stroke using BE-FAST and act.
Assess tone, motor control, balance and gait with standardised measures.
Apply task-specific, high-repetition training.
Protect the shoulder and prevent complications.
